question: when was coffee first made into a drink
gold_text: in the middle of the 15th century, in Yemen 's Sufi monasteries. [1] Coffee beans were first exported from Ethiopia to Yemen . Yemeni traders brought coffee back to their homeland and began to cultivate the bean. [13] The word qahwa originally meant wine, and Sufis in Yemen used the beverage as an aid to concentration and as a kind of spiritual intoxication when they chanted the name of God. [14] Sufis used it to keep themselves alert during their nighttime devotions. A translation of Al-Jaziri's manuscript [15] traces the spread of coffee from Arabia Felix (the present day Yemen) northward to Mecca and Medina , and then to the larger cities of Cairo , Damascus , Baghdad , and Constantinople . By 1414, the beverage was known in Mecca, and in the early 1500s was spreading to the Mameluke Sultanate of Egypt and North Africa from the Yemeni port of Mocha . [8] [14] Associated with Sufism , a myriad of coffee houses grew up in Cairo (Egypt) around the religious University of the Azhar. These coffee houses also opened in Syria, especially in the cosmopolitan city of Aleppo, [14] and then in Istanbul, the capital of the Ottoman Empire , in 1554. [14] In 1511, it was forbidden for its stimulating effect by conservative, orthodox imams at a theological court in Mecca . [16] However, these bans were to be overturned in 1524 by an order of the Ottoman Turkish Sultan Suleiman I , with Grand Mufti Mehmet Ebussuud el-İmadi issuing a fatwa allowing the consumption of coffee. [17] In Cairo , Egypt, a similar ban was instituted in 1532, and the coffeehouses and warehouses containing coffee beans were sacked. [18] During the 16th century, it had already reached the rest of the Middle East, the Safavid Empire and the Ottoman Empire . From the Middle East, coffee drinking spread to Italy, then to the rest of Europe, and coffee plants were transported by the Dutch to the East Indies and to the Americas. [2] Similarly, coffee was banned by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church some time before the 18th century. [19]
model_answer: Coffee was first made into a drink in the middle of the 15th century in Yemen's Sufi monasteries.

question: when was coffee first made into a drink
gold_text: in the middle of the 15th century, in Yemen 's Sufi monasteries. [1] Coffee beans were first exported from Ethiopia to Yemen . Yemeni traders brought coffee back to their homeland and began to cultivate the bean. [13] The word qahwa originally meant wine, and Sufis in Yemen used the beverage as an aid to concentration and as a kind of spiritual intoxication when they chanted the name of God. [14] Sufis used it to keep themselves alert during their nighttime devotions. A translation of Al-Jaziri's manuscript [15] traces the spread of coffee from Arabia Felix (the present day Yemen) northward to Mecca and Medina , and then to the larger cities of Cairo , Damascus , Baghdad , and Constantinople . By 1414, the beverage was known in Mecca, and in the early 1500s was spreading to the Mameluke Sultanate of Egypt and North Africa from the Yemeni port of Mocha . [8] [14] Associated with Sufism , a myriad of coffee houses grew up in Cairo (Egypt) around the religious University of the Azhar. These coffee houses also opened in Syria, especially in the cosmopolitan city of Aleppo, [14] and then in Istanbul, the capital of the Ottoman Empire , in 1554. [14] In 1511, it was forbidden for its stimulating effect by conservative, orthodox imams at a theological court in Mecca . [16] However, these bans were to be overturned in 1524 by an order of the Ottoman Turkish Sultan Suleiman I , with Grand Mufti Mehmet Ebussuud el-İmadi issuing a fatwa allowing the consumption of coffee. [17] In Cairo , Egypt, a similar ban was instituted in 1532, and the coffeehouses and warehouses containing coffee beans were sacked. [18] During the 16th century, it had already reached the rest of the Middle East, the Safavid Empire and the Ottoman Empire . From the Middle East, coffee drinking spread to Italy, then to the rest of Europe, and coffee plants were transported by the Dutch to the East Indies and to the Americas. [2] Similarly, coffee was banned by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church some time before the 18th century. [19]
model_answer: Coffee was first made into a drink in the middle of the 15th century in Yemen's Sufi monasteries.

question: when was coffee first made into a drink
gold_text: in the middle of the 15th century, in Yemen 's Sufi monasteries. [1] Coffee beans were first exported from Ethiopia to Yemen . Yemeni traders brought coffee back to their homeland and began to cultivate the bean. [13] The word qahwa originally meant wine, and Sufis in Yemen used the beverage as an aid to concentration and as a kind of spiritual intoxication when they chanted the name of God. [14] Sufis used it to keep themselves alert during their nighttime devotions. A translation of Al-Jaziri's manuscript [15] traces the spread of coffee from Arabia Felix (the present day Yemen) northward to Mecca and Medina , and then to the larger cities of Cairo , Damascus , Baghdad , and Constantinople . By 1414, the beverage was known in Mecca, and in the early 1500s was spreading to the Mameluke Sultanate of Egypt and North Africa from the Yemeni port of Mocha . [8] [14] Associated with Sufism , a myriad of coffee houses grew up in Cairo (Egypt) around the religious University of the Azhar. These coffee houses also opened in Syria, especially in the cosmopolitan city of Aleppo, [14] and then in Istanbul, the capital of the Ottoman Empire , in 1554. [14] In 1511, it was forbidden for its stimulating effect by conservative, orthodox imams at a theological court in Mecca . [16] However, these bans were to be overturned in 1524 by an order of the Ottoman Turkish Sultan Suleiman I , with Grand Mufti Mehmet Ebussuud el-İmadi issuing a fatwa allowing the consumption of coffee. [17] In Cairo , Egypt, a similar ban was instituted in 1532, and the coffeehouses and warehouses containing coffee beans were sacked. [18] During the 16th century, it had already reached the rest of the Middle East, the Safavid Empire and the Ottoman Empire . From the Middle East, coffee drinking spread to Italy, then to the rest of Europe, and coffee plants were transported by the Dutch to the East Indies and to the Americas. [2] Similarly, coffee was banned by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church some time before the 18th century. [19]
model_answer: Coffee was first made into a drink in the middle of the 15th century in Yemen's Sufi monasteries.

retention in time. This curve shows how information is lost over time when there is no attempt to retain it. [1] A related concept is the strength of memory that refers to the durability that memory traces in the brain . The stronger the memory, the longer period of time that a person is able to recall it. A typical graph of the forgetting curve purports to show that humans tend to halve their memory of newly learned knowledge in a matter of days or weeks unless they consciously review the learned material. The forgetting curve supports one of the seven kinds of memory failures: transience, which is the process of forgetting that occurs with the passage of time. [2] Contents [ hide ] 1 History 2 Description 3 4 Notes 5 History [ edit ] In 1885, Hermann Ebbinghaus collected data to plot a forgetting curve. Today, we approximate forgetting with an exponential curve [3] : R = e − t S , {\displaystyle R=e^{-{\frac {t}{S}}},} where R {\displaystyle R} is retrievability (a measure of how easy it is to retrieve a piece of information from memory), S {\displaystyle S} is stability of memory (determines how fast R {\displaystyle R} falls over time in the absence of training, testing or other recall), and t {\displaystyle t} is time. Hermann Ebbinghaus ran a limited, incomplete study on himself and published his hypothesis in 1885 as Über das Gedächtnis (later translated into English as Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology ). Ebbinghaus studied the memorisation of nonsense syllables, such as "WID" and "ZOF" (CVCs or Consonant-Vowel-Consonant) by repeatedly testing himself after various time periods and recording the results. He plotted these results on a graph creating what is now known as the "forgetting curve". From his discovery regarding the "forgetting curve", Ebbinghaus came up with the effects of "overlearning". Essentially, if you practiced something more than what is usually necessary to memorize it, you would have effectively achieved overlearning. [1] A related concept is the strength of memory that refers to the durability that memory traces in the brain . The stronger the memory, the longer period of time that a person is able to recall it. A typical graph of the forgetting curve purports to show that humans tend to halve their memory of newly learned knowledge in a matter of days or weeks unless they consciously review the learned material. The forgetting curve supports one of the seven kinds of memory failures: transience, which is the process of forgetting that occurs with the passage of time. Hermann Ebbinghaus ran a limited, incomplete study on himself and published his hypothesis in 1885 as Über das Gedächtnis (later translated into English as Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology ). gold_text: retention in time. This curve shows how information is lost over time when there is no attempt to retain it. [1] A related concept is the strength of memory that refers to the durability that memory traces in the brain . The stronger the memory, the longer period of time that a person is able to recall it. A typical graph of the forgetting curve purports to show that humans tend to halve their memory of newly learned knowledge in a matter of days or weeks unless they consciously review the learned material. The forgetting curve supports one of the seven kinds of memory failures: transience, which is the process of forgetting that occurs with the passage of time. Hermann Ebbinghaus ran a limited, incomplete study on himself and published his hypothesis in 1885 as Über das Gedächtnis (later translated into English as Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology ). Ebbinghaus studied the memorisation of nonsense syllables, such as "WID" and "ZOF" (CVCs or Consonant-Vowel-Consonant) by repeatedly testing himself after various time periods and recording the results. He plotted these results on a graph creating what is now known as the "forgetting curve". From his discovery regarding the "forgetting curve", Ebbinghaus came up with the effects of "overlearning". Essentially, if you practiced something more than what is usually necessary to memorize it, you would have effectively achieved overlearning. [1] A related concept is the strength of memory that refers to the durability that memory traces in the brain . The stronger the memory, the longer period of time that a person is able to recall it. A typical graph of the forgetting curve purports to show that humans tend to halve their memory of newly learned knowledge in a matter of days or weeks unless they consciously review the learned material. The forgetting curve supports one of the seven kinds of memory failures: transience, which is the process of forgetting that occurs with the passage of time. Hermann Ebbinghaus ran a limited, incomplete study on himself and published his hypothesis in 1885 as Über das Gedächtnis (later translated into English as Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology ). The forgetting curve supports one of the seven kinds of memory failures: transience, which is the process of forgetting that occurs with the passage of time. [1] A related concept is the strength of memory that refers to the durability that memory traces in the brain . The stronger the memory, the longer period of time that a person is able to recall it. A typical graph of the forgetting curve purports to show that humans tend to halve their memory of newly learned knowledge in a matter of days or weeks unless they consciously review the learned material. The forgetting curve supports one of the seven kinds of memory failures: transience, which is the process of forgetting that occurs with the passage of time. Hermann Ebbinghaus ran a limited, incomplete study on himself and published his hypothesis in 1885 as Über das Gedächtnis (later translated into English as Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology ). [1] A related concept is the strength of memory that refers to the durability that memory traces in the brain . The stronger the memory, the longer period of time that a person is able to recall it. A typical graph of the forgetting curve purports to show that humans tend to halve their memory of newly learned knowledge in a matter of days or weeks unless they consciously review the learned material. The forgetting curve supports one of the seven kinds of memory failures: transience, which is the process of forgetting that occurs with the passage of time. Hermann Ebbinghaus ran a limited, incomplete study on himself and published his hypothesis in 1885 as Über das Gedächtnis (later translated into English as Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology ). The forgetting curve supports one of the seven kinds of memory failures: transience, which is the process of forgetting that occurs with the passage of time. [1] A related concept is the strength of memory that refers to the durability that memory traces in the brain . The stronger the memory, the longer period of time that a person is able to recall it. A typical graph of the forgetting curve purports to show that humans tend to halve their memory of newly learned knowledge in a matter of days or weeks unless they consciously review the learned material. The forgetting curve supports one of the seven kinds of memory failures: transience, which is the process of forgetting that occurs with the passage of time. [2] Contents [ hide ] 1 History 2 Description 3 4 Notes 5 History [ edit ] In 1885, Hermann Ebbinghaus collected data to plot a forgetting curve. Today, we approximate forgetting with an exponential curve [3] : R = e − t S , {\displaystyle R=e^{-{\frac {t}{S}}},} where R {\displaystyle R} is retrievability (a measure of how easy it is to retrieve a piece of information from memory), S {\displaystyle S} is stability of memory (determines how fast R {\displaystyle R} falls over time in the absence of training, testing or other recall), and t {\displaystyle t} is time. Hermann Ebbinghaus ran a limited, incomplete study on himself and published his hypothesis in 1885 as Über das Gedächtnis (later translated into English as Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology ). Ebbinghaus studied the memorisation of nonsense syllables, such as "WID" and "ZOF" (CVCs or Consonant-Vowel-Consonant) by repeatedly testing himself after various time periods and recording the results. He plotted these results on a graph creating what is now known as the "forgetting curve". From his discovery regarding the "forgetting curve", Ebbinghaus came up with the effects of "overlearning". Essentially, if you practiced something more than what is usually necessary to memorize it, you would have effectively achieved overlearning. Overlearning ensures that information is more impervious to being lost or forgotten, and the forgetting curve for this overlearned material is shallower. [4] In

The term "toddler" is derived from "to toddle," which means to walk unsteadily, like a child of this age. The development of a toddler can be broken down into various interrelated areas, including physical, motor, vocalization and socialization, and emotional development.

At one year of age, a typical toddler will be able to display various skills, such as walking, feeding themselves, and manipulating objects. By two years old, a toddler's language skills will have significantly improved, and they will begin to engage in parallel play with other children. By two and a half years old, a toddler will have developed more advanced motor skills, such as running and climbing, and will be able to take turns during play.

It is important to note that while there are general developmental milestones for toddlers, individual differences between children are common. A toddler is typically considered to be a child between the ages of 1 and 3. This period is marked by significant cognitive, emotional, and social development. The term "toddler" is derived from "to toddle," which means to walk unsteadily, like a child of this age. The development of a toddler can be broken down into various interrelated areas, including physical, motor, vocalization and socialization, and emotional development.

At one year of age, a typical toddler will be able to display various skills, such as walking, feeding themselves, and manipulating objects. By two years old, a toddler's physical growth and motor skills have significantly improved, allowing them to run, jump, and climb. Their vocalization and socialization skills also develop, as they learn to take turns during play and engage in fantasy play.

It is important to recognize that development exists on a continuum, with considerable individual differences between children. While these are general milestones, it is essential to remember that each child develops at their own pace.

A toddler is typically considered to be a child between the ages of 1 and 3. This period is marked by significant cognitive, emotional, and social development. The term "toddler" is derived from "to toddle," which means to walk unsteadily, like a child of this age. The development of a toddler can be broken down into various interrelated areas, including physical, motor, vocalization and socialization, and emotional development.

At one year of age, a typical toddler will be able to display various skills, such as walking, understanding simple instructions, and beginning to use words to communicate. By two years old, a toddler's vocabulary and motor skills will have significantly improved, and they will start to engage in parallel play with other children. By two and a half years old, a toddler will have developed more advanced motor skills, such as running and climbing, and will be able to engage in more complex social interactions.

It is important to note that development exists on a continuum, and there is considerable individual variation between children. Some children may reach these milestones earlier or later than others, and this is considered normal. If you have concerns about your child's development, it is always a good idea to consult with a healthcare professional.

In terms of age, a toddler is no longer considered a toddler once they reach the age of 3. At this point, they transition into the preschool age range. However, the term "toddler" is often used more broadly to refer to young children in general, and it is not uncommon to hear the term used to describe children up to the age of 5 or 6.

At two years old, a toddler's physical growth and motor skills continue to develop, and they may begin to use language more effectively. At two and a half years old, a toddler's motor development, language skills, and emotional and self-image development continue to progress.

[143] Human intake varies depending on location and diet. Lithium was first detected in human organs and fetal tissues in the late 19th century. In humans there are no defined lithium deficiency diseases, but low lithium intakes from water supplies were associated with increased rates of suicides, homicides and the arrest rates for drug use and other crimes. The biochemical mechanisms of action of lithium appear to be multifactorial and are intercorrelated with the functions of several enzymes, hormones and vitamins, as well as with growth and transforming factors. Evidence now appears to be sufficient to accept lithium as essential; a provisional RDA of 1,000 µg/day is suggested for a 70 kg adult. [143] [144] Precautions [ edit ] NFPA 704 fire diamond 3 2 2 W Fire diamond hazard sign for lithium metal [145] Lithium is corrosive and requires special handling to avoid skin contact. Breathing lithium dust or lithium compounds (which are often alkaline) initially irritate the nose and throat, while higher exposure can cause a buildup of fluid in the lungs , leading to pulmonary edema . The metal itself is a handling hazard because contact with moisture produces the caustic lithium hydroxide. Lithium is safely stored in non-reactive compounds such as naphtha . [139] Medicine [ edit ] Main article: Lithium (medication) Lithium is useful in the treatment of bipolar disorder . [140] Lithium salts may also be helpful for related diagnoses, such as schizoaffective disorder and cyclic major depression . The active part of these salts is the lithium ion Li + . [140] They may increase the risk of developing Ebstein's cardiac anomaly in infants born to women who take lithium during the first trimester of pregnancy. [141] Lithium has also been researched as a possible treatment for cluster headaches . [142] Biological role [ edit ] Primary food sources of lithium are grains and vegetables, and, in some areas, drinking water also contains significant amounts. [143] Human intake varies depending on location and diet. Lithium was first detected in human organs and fetal tissues in the late 19th century. In humans there are no defined lithium deficiency diseases, but low lithium intakes from water supplies were associated with increased rates of suicides, homicides and the arrest rates for drug use and other crimes. The biochemical mechanisms of action of lithium appear to be multifactorial and are intercorrelated with the functions of several enzymes, hormones and vitamins, as well as with growth and transforming factors. Evidence now appears to be sufficient to accept lithium as essential; a provisional RDA of 1,000 µg/day is suggested for a 70 kg adult. [143] [144] Precautions [ edit ] NFPA 704 fire diamond 3 2 2 W Fire diamond hazard sign for lithium metal [145] Lithium is corrosive and requires special handling to avoid skin contact. Breathing lithium dust or lithium compounds (which are often alkaline) initially irritate the nose and throat, while higher exposure can cause a buildup of fluid in the lungs , leading to pulmonary edema . The metal itself is a handling hazard because contact with moisture produces the caustic lithium hydroxide. Lithium is safely stored in non-reactive compounds such as naphtha . [146] Regulation [ edit ] Some jurisdictions limit the sale of lithium batteries , which are the most readily available source of lithium for ordinary consumers. Lithium
model_answer: The main mineral in lithium batteries is lithium itself, in the form of lithium ions (Li+). These ions are stored in the cathode and move to the anode during discharge, providing the energy needed to power the device.

[139] Medicine [ edit ] Main article: Lithium (medication) Lithium is useful in the treatment of bipolar disorder . [140] Lithium salts may also be helpful for related diagnoses, such as schizoaffective disorder and cyclic major depression . The active part of these salts is the lithium ion Li + . [140] They may increase the risk of developing Ebstein's cardiac anomaly in infants born to women who take lithium during the first trimester of pregnancy. [141] Lithium has also been researched as a possible treatment for cluster headaches . [142] Biological role [ edit ] Primary food sources of lithium are grains and vegetables, and, in some areas, drinking water also contains significant amounts. [143] Human intake varies depending on location and diet. Lithium was first detected in human organs and fetal tissues in the late 19th century. In humans there are no defined lithium deficiency diseases, but low lithium intakes from water supplies were associated with increased rates of suicides, homicides and the arrest rates for drug use and other crimes. The biochemical mechanisms of action of lithium appear to be multifactorial and are intercorrelated with the functions of several enzymes, hormones and vitamins, as well as with growth and transforming factors. Evidence now appears to be sufficient to accept lithium as essential; a provisional RDA of 1,000 µg/day is suggested for a 70 kg adult. [143] [144] Precautions [ edit ] NFPA 704 fire diamond 3 2 2 W Fire diamond hazard sign for lithium metal [145] Lithium is corrosive and requires special handling to avoid skin contact. Breathing lithium dust or lithium compounds (which are often alkaline) initially irritate the nose and throat, while higher exposure can cause a buildup of fluid in the lungs , leading to pulmonary edema . The metal itself is a handling hazard because contact with moisture produces the caustic lithium hydroxide. Lithium is safely stored in non-reactive compounds such as naphtha . [146] Regulation [ edit ] Some jurisdictions limit the sale of lithium batteries , which are the most readily available source of lithium for ordinary consumers. Lithium

[139] Medicine [ edit ] Main article: Lithium (medication) Lithium is useful in the treatment of bipolar disorder . [140] Lithium salts may also be helpful for related diagnoses, such as schizoaffective disorder and cyclic major depression . The active part of these salts is the lithium ion Li + . [140] They may increase the risk of developing Ebstein's cardiac anomaly in infants born to women who take lithium during the first trimester of pregnancy. [141] Lithium has also been researched as a possible treatment for cluster headaches . [142] Biological role [ edit ] Primary food sources of lithium are grains and vegetables, and, in some areas, drinking water also contains significant amounts. [143] Human intake varies depending on location and diet. Lithium was first detected in human organs and fetal tissues in the late 19th century. In humans there are no defined lithium deficiency diseases, but low lithium intakes from water supplies were associated with increased rates of suicides, homicides and the arrest rates for drug use and other crimes. The biochemical mechanisms of action of lithium appear to be multifactorial and are intercorrelated with the functions of several enzymes, hormones and vitamins, as well as with growth and transforming factors. Evidence now appears to be sufficient to accept lithium as essential; a provisional RDA of 1,000 µg/day is suggested for a 70 kg adult. [143] [144] Precautions [ edit ] NFPA 704 fire diamond 3 2 2 W Fire diamond hazard sign for lithium metal [145] Lithium is corrosive and requires special handling to avoid skin contact. Breathing lithium dust or lithium compounds (which are often alkaline) initially irritate the nose and throat, while higher exposure can cause a buildup of fluid in the lungs , leading to pulmonary edema . The metal itself is a handling hazard because contact with moisture produces the caustic lithium hydroxide. Lithium is safely stored in non-reactive compounds such as naphtha . [146] Regulation [ edit ] Some jurisdictions limit the sale of lithium batteries , which are the most readily available source of lithium for ordinary consumers. Lithium

[139] Medicine [ edit ] Main article: Lithium (medication) Lithium is useful in the treatment of bipolar disorder . [140] Lithium salts may also be helpful for related diagnoses, such as schizoaffective disorder and cyclic major depression . The active part of these salts is the lithium ion Li + . [140] They may increase the risk of developing Ebstein's cardiac anomaly in infants born to women who take lithium during the first trimester of pregnancy. [141] Lithium has also been researched as a possible treatment for cluster headaches . [142] Biological role [ edit ] Primary food sources of lithium are grains and vegetables, and, in some areas, drinking water also contains significant amounts. [143] Human intake varies depending on location and diet. Lithium was first detected in human organs and fetal tissues in the late 19th century. In humans there are no defined lithium deficiency diseases, but low lithium intakes from water supplies were associated with increased rates of suicides, homicides and the arrest rates for drug use and other crimes. The biochemical mechanisms of action of lithium appear to be multifactorial and are intercorrelated with the functions of several enzymes, hormones and vitamins, as well as with growth and transforming factors. Evidence now appears to be sufficient to accept lithium as essential; a provisional RDA of 1,000 µg/day is suggested for a 70 kg adult. [143] [144] Precautions [ edit ] NFPA 704 fire diamond 3 2 2 W Fire diamond hazard sign for lithium metal [145] Lithium is corrosive and requires special handling to avoid skin contact. Breathing lithium dust or lithium compounds (which are often alkaline) initially irritate the nose and throat, while higher exposure can cause a buildup of fluid in the lungs , leading to pulmonary edema . The metal itself is a handling hazard because contact with moisture produces the caustic lithium hydroxide. Lithium is safely stored in non-reactive compounds such as naphtha . [146] Regulation [ edit ] Some jurisdictions limit the sale of lithium batteries , which are the most readily available source of lithium for ordinary consumers. Lithium
model_answer: The main mineral in lithium batteries is lithium itself. Lithium-ion batteries use lithium ions that move between the anode and cathode during charging and discharging cycles. The cathode is typically made of a lithium compound, such as lithium cobalt oxide, lithium iron phosphate, or lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide. The anode is usually made of graphite.

gold_text: exchangers that are prone to corrosion. The reactors use lithium to counteract the corrosive effects of boric acid , which is added to the water to absorb excess neutrons. [139] Medicine [ edit ] Main article: Lithium (medication) Lithium is useful in the treatment of bipolar disorder . [140] Lithium salts may also be helpful for related diagnoses, such as schizoaffective disorder and cyclic major depression . The active part of these salts is the lithium ion Li + . [140] They may increase the risk of developing Ebstein's cardiac anomaly in infants born to women who take lithium during the first trimester of pregnancy. [141] Lithium has also been researched as a possible treatment for cluster headaches . [142] Biological role [ edit ] Primary food sources of lithium are grains and vegetables, and, in some areas, drinking water also contains significant amounts. [143] Human intake varies depending on location and diet. Lithium was first detected in human organs and fetal tissues in the late 19th century. In humans there are no defined lithium deficiency diseases, but low lithium intakes from water supplies were associated with increased rates of suicides, homicides and the arrest rates for drug use and other crimes. The biochemical mechanisms of action of lithium appear to be multifactorial and are intercorrelated with the functions of several enzymes, hormones and vitamins, as well as with growth and transforming factors. Evidence now appears to be sufficient to accept lithium as essential; a provisional RDA of 1,000 µg/day is suggested for a 70 kg adult. [143] [144] Precautions [ edit ] NFPA 704 fire diamond 3 2 2 W Fire diamond hazard sign for lithium metal [145] Lithium is corrosive and requires special handling to avoid skin contact. Breathing lithium dust or lithium compounds (which are often alkaline) initially irritate the nose and throat, while higher exposure can cause a buildup of fluid in the lungs , leading to pulmonary edema . The metal itself is a handling hazard because contact with moisture produces the caustic lithium hydroxide. Lithium is safely stored in non-reactive compounds such as naphtha . [146] Regulation [ edit ] Some jurisdictions limit the sale of lithium batteries , which are the most readily available source of lithium for ordinary consumers. Lithium

gold_text: exchangers that are prone to corrosion. The reactors use lithium to counteract the corrosive effects of boric acid , which is added to the water to absorb excess neutrons. [139] Medicine [ edit ] Main article: Lithium (medication) Lithium is useful in the treatment of bipolar disorder . [140] Lithium salts may also be helpful for related diagnoses, such as schizoaffective disorder and cyclic major depression . The active part of these salts is the lithium ion Li + . [140] They may increase the risk of developing Ebstein's cardiac anomaly in infants born to women who take lithium during the first trimester of pregnancy. [141] Lithium has also been researched as a possible treatment for cluster headaches . [142] Biological role [ edit ] Primary food sources of lithium are grains and vegetables, and, in some areas, drinking water also contains significant amounts. [143] Human intake varies depending on location and diet. Lithium was first detected in human organs and fetal tissues in the late 19th century. In humans there are no defined lithium deficiency diseases, but low lithium intakes from water supplies were associated with increased rates of suicides, homicides and the arrest rates for drug use and other crimes. The biochemical mechanisms of action of lithium appear to be multifactorial and are intercorrelated with the functions of several enzymes, hormones and vitamins, as well as with growth and transforming factors. Evidence now appears to be sufficient to accept lithium as essential; a provisional RDA of 1,000 µg/day is suggested for a 70 kg adult. [143] [144] Precautions [ edit ] NFPA 704 fire diamond 3 2 2 W Fire diamond hazard sign for lithium metal [145] Lithium is corrosive and requires special handling to avoid skin contact. Breathing lithium dust or lithium compounds (which are often alkaline) initially irritate the nose and throat, while higher exposure can cause a buildup of fluid in the lungs , leading to pulmonary edema . The metal itself is a handling hazard because contact with moisture produces the caustic lithium hydroxide. Lithium is safely stored in non-reactive compounds such as naphtha . [146] Regulation [ edit ] Some jurisdictions limit the sale of lithium batteries , which are the most readily available source of lithium for ordinary consumers. Lithium

gold_text: exchangers that are prone to corrosion. The reactors use lithium to counteract the corrosive effects of boric acid , which is added to the water to absorb excess neutrons. [139] Medicine [ edit ] Main article: Lithium (medication) Lithium is useful in the treatment of bipolar disorder . [140] Lithium salts may also be helpful for related diagnoses, such as schizoaffective disorder and cyclic major depression . The active part of these salts is the lithium ion Li + . [140] They may increase the risk of developing Ebstein's cardiac anomaly in infants born to women who take lithium during the first trimester of pregnancy. [141] Lithium has also been researched as a possible treatment for cluster headaches . [142] Biological role [ edit ] Primary food sources of lithium are grains and vegetables, and, in some areas, drinking water also contains significant amounts. [143] Human intake varies depending on location and diet. Lithium was first detected in human organs and fetal tissues in the late 19th century. In humans there are no defined lithium deficiency diseases, but low lithium intakes from water supplies were associated with increased rates of suicides, homicides and the arrest rates for drug use and other crimes. The biochemical mechanisms of action of lithium appear to be multifactorial and are intercorrelated with the functions of several enzymes, hormones and vitamins, as well as with growth and transforming factors. Evidence now appears to be sufficient to accept lithium as essential; a provisional RDA of 1,000 µg/day is suggested for a 70 kg adult. [143] [144] Precautions [ edit ] NFPA 704 fire diamond 3 2 2 W Fire diamond hazard sign for lithium metal [145] Lithium is corrosive and requires special handling to avoid skin contact. Breathing lithium dust or lithium compounds (which are often alkaline) initially irritate the nose and throat, while higher exposure can cause a buildup of fluid in the lungs , leading to pulmonary edema . The metal itself is a handling hazard because contact with moisture produces the caustic lithium hydroxide. Lithium is safely stored in non-reactive compounds such as naphtha . [146] Regulation [ edit ] Some jurisdictions limit the sale of lithium batteries , which are the most readily available source of lithium for ordinary consumers. Lithium

gold_text: exchangers that are prone to corrosion. The reactors use lithium to counteract the corrosive effects of boric acid , which is added to the water to absorb excess neutrons. [139] Medicine [ edit ] Main article: Lithium (medication) Lithium is useful in the treatment of bipolar disorder . [140] Lithium salts may also be helpful for related diagnoses, such as schizoaffective disorder and cyclic major depression . The active part of these salts is the lithium ion Li + . [140] They may increase the risk of developing Ebstein's cardiac anomaly in infants born to women who take lithium during the first trimester of pregnancy. [141] Lithium has also been researched as a possible treatment for cluster headaches . [142] Biological role [ edit ] Primary food sources of lithium are grains and vegetables, and, in some areas, drinking water also contains significant amounts. [143] Human intake varies depending on location and diet. Lithium was first detected in human organs and fetal tissues in the late 19th century. In humans there are no defined lithium deficiency diseases, but low lithium intakes from water supplies were associated with increased rates of suicides, homicides and the arrest rates for drug use and other crimes. The biochemical mechanisms of action of lithium appear to be multifactorial and are intercorrelated with the functions of several enzymes, hormones and vitamins, as well as with growth and transforming factors. Evidence now appears to be sufficient to accept lithium as essential; a provisional RDA of 1,000 µg/day is suggested for a 70 kg adult. [143] [144] Precautions [ edit ] NFPA 704 fire diamond 3 2 2 W Fire diamond hazard sign for lithium metal [145] Lithium is corrosive and requires special handling to avoid skin contact. Breathing lithium dust or lithium compounds (which are often alkaline) initially irritate the nose and throat, while higher exposure can cause a buildup of fluid in the lungs , leading to pulmonary edema . The metal itself is a handling hazard because contact with moisture produces the caustic lithium hydroxide. Lithium is safely stored in non-reactive compounds such as naphtha . [146] Regulation [ edit ] Some jurisdictions limit the sale of lithium batteries , which are the most readily available source of lithium for ordinary consumers. Lithium

gold_text: exchangers that are prone to corrosion. The reactors use lithium to counteract the corrosive effects of boric acid , which is added to the water to absorb excess neutrons. [139] Medicine [ edit ] Main article: Lithium (medication) Lithium is useful in the treatment of bipolar disorder . [140] Lithium salts may also be helpful for related diagnoses, such as schizoaffective disorder and cyclic major depression . The active part of these salts is the lithium ion Li + . [140] They may increase the risk of developing Ebstein's cardiac anomaly in infants born to women who take lithium during the first trimester of pregnancy. [141] Lithium has also been researched as a possible treatment for cluster headaches . [142] Biological role [ edit ] Primary food sources of lithium are grains and vegetables, and, in some areas, drinking water also contains significant amounts. [143] Human intake varies depending on location and diet. Lithium was first detected in human organs and fetal tissues in the late 19th century. In humans there are no defined lithium deficiency diseases, but low lithium intakes from water supplies were associated with increased rates of suicides, homicides and the arrest rates for drug use and other crimes. The biochemical mechanisms of action of lithium appear to be multifactorial and are intercorrelated with the functions of several enzymes, hormones and vitamins, as well as with growth and transforming factors. Evidence now appears to be sufficient to accept lithium as essential; a provisional RDA of 1,000 µg/day is suggested for a 70 kg adult. [143] [144] Precautions [ edit ] NFPA 704 fire diamond 3 2 2 W Fire diamond hazard sign for lithium metal [145] Lithium is corrosive and requires special handling to avoid skin contact. Breathing lithium dust or lithium compounds (which are often alkaline) initially irritate the nose and throat, while higher exposure can cause a buildup of fluid in the lungs , leading to pulmonary edema . The metal itself is a handling hazard because contact with moisture produces the caustic lithium hydroxide. Lithium is safely stored in non-reactive compounds such as naphtha . [146] Regulation [ edit ] Some jurisdictions limit the sale of lithium batteries , which are the most readily available source of lithium for ordinary consumers. Lithium

gold_text: exchangers that are prone to corrosion. The reactors use lithium to counteract the corrosive effects of boric acid , which is added to the water to absorb excess neutrons. [139] Medicine [ edit ] Main article: Lithium (medication) Lithium is useful in the treatment of bipolar disorder . [140] Lithium salts may also be helpful for related diagnoses, such as schizoaffective disorder and cyclic major depression . The active part of these salts is the lithium ion Li + . [140] They may increase the risk of developing Ebstein's cardiac anomaly in infants born to women who take lithium during the first trimester of pregnancy. [141] Lithium has also been researched as a possible treatment for cluster headaches . [142] Biological role [ edit ] Primary food sources of lithium are grains and vegetables, and, in some areas, drinking water also contains significant amounts. [143] Human intake varies depending on location and diet. Lithium was first detected in human organs and fetal tissues in the late 19th century. In humans there are no defined lithium deficiency diseases, but low lithium intakes from water supplies were associated with increased rates of suicides, homicides and the arrest rates for drug use and other crimes. The biochemical mechanisms of action of lithium appear to be multifactorial and are intercorrelated with the functions of several enzymes, hormones and vitamins, as well as with growth and transforming factors. Evidence now appears to be sufficient to accept lithium as essential; a provisional RDA of 1,000 µg/day is suggested for a 70 kg adult. [143] [144] Precautions [ edit ] NFPA 704 fire diamond 3 2 2 W Fire diamond hazard sign for lithium metal [145] Lithium is corrosive and requires special handling to avoid skin contact. Breathing lithium dust or lithium compounds (which are often alkaline) initially irritate the nose and throat, while higher exposure can cause a buildup of fluid in the lungs , leading to pulmonary edema . The metal itself is a handling hazard because contact with moisture produces the caustic lithium hydroxide. Lithium is safely stored in non-reactive compounds such as naphtha . [146] Regulation [ edit ] Some jurisdictions limit the sale of lithium batteries , which are the most readily available source of lithium for ordinary consumers. Lithium

gold_text: exchangers that are prone to corrosion. The reactors use lithium to counteract the corrosive effects of boric acid , which is added to the water to absorb excess neutrons. [139] Medicine [ edit ] Main article: Lithium (medication) Lithium is useful in the treatment of bipolar disorder . [140] Lithium salts may also be helpful for related diagnoses, such as schizoaffective disorder and cyclic major depression . The active part of these salts is the lithium ion Li + . [140] They may increase the risk of developing Ebstein's cardiac anomaly in infants born to women who take lithium during the first trimester of pregnancy. [141] Lithium has also been researched as a possible treatment for cluster headaches . [142] Biological role [ edit ] Primary food sources of lithium are grains and vegetables, and, in some areas, drinking water also contains significant amounts. [143] Human intake varies depending on location and diet. Lithium was first detected in human organs and fetal tissues in the late 19th century. In humans there are no defined lithium deficiency diseases, but low lithium intakes from water supplies were associated with increased rates of suicides, homicides and the arrest rates for drug use and other crimes. The biochemical mechanisms of action of lithium appear to be multifactorial and are intercorrelated with the functions of several enzymes, hormones and vitamins, as well as with growth and transforming factors. Evidence now appears to be sufficient to accept lithium as essential; a provisional RDA of 1,000 µg/day is suggested for a 70 kg adult. [143] [144] Precautions [ edit ] NFPA 704 fire diamond 3 2 2 W Fire diamond hazard sign for lithium metal [145] Lithium is corrosive and requires special handling to avoid skin contact. Breathing lithium dust or lithium compounds (which are often alkaline) initially irritate the nose and throat, while higher exposure can cause a buildup of fluid in the lungs , leading to pulmonary edema . The metal itself is a handling hazard because contact with moisture produces the caustic lithium hydroxide. Lithium is safely stored in non-reactive compounds such as naphtha . [146] Regulation [ edit ] Some jurisdictions limit the sale of lithium batteries , which are the most readily available source of lithium for ordinary consumers. Lithium

question: what is the main mineral in lithium batteries
gold_text: exchangers that are prone to corrosion. The reactors use lithium to counteract the corrosive effects of boric acid , which is added to the water to absorb excess neutrons. [139] Medicine [ edit ] Main article: Lithium (medication) Lithium is useful in the treatment of bipolar disorder . [140] Lithium salts may also be helpful for related diagnoses, such as schizoaffective disorder and cyclic major depression . The active part of these salts is the lithium ion Li + . [140] They may increase the risk of developing Ebstein's cardiac anomaly in infants born to women who take lithium during the first trimester of pregnancy. [141] Lithium has also been researched as a possible treatment for cluster headaches . [142] Biological role [ edit ] Primary food sources of lithium are grains and vegetables, and, in some areas, drinking water also contains significant amounts. [143] Human intake varies depending on location and diet. Lithium was first detected in human organs and fetal tissues in the late 19th century. In humans there are no defined lithium deficiency diseases, but low lithium intakes from water supplies were associated with increased rates of suicides, homicides and the arrest rates for drug use and other crimes. The biochemical mechanisms of action of lithium appear to be multifactorial and are intercorrelated with the functions of several enzymes, hormones and vitamins, as well as with growth and transforming factors. Evidence now appears to be sufficient to accept lithium as essential; a provisional RDA of 1,000 µg/day is suggested for a 70 kg adult. [143] [144] Precautions [ edit ] NFPA 704 fire diamond 3 2 2 W Fire diamond hazard sign for lithium metal [145] Lithium is corrosive and requires special handling to avoid skin contact. Breathing lithium dust or lithium compounds (which are often alkaline) initially irritate the nose and throat, while higher exposure can cause a buildup of fluid in the lungs , leading to pulmonary edema . The metal itself is a handling hazard because contact with moisture produces the caustic lithium hydroxide. Lithium is safely stored in non-reactive compounds such as naphtha . [146] Regulation [ edit ] Some jurisdictions limit the sale of lithium batteries , which are the most readily available source of lithium for ordinary consumers. Lithium
model_answer: The main mineral in lithium batteries is lithium itself, in the form of lithium ions (Li+). These ions are used in the cathode of lithium-ion batteries, where they react with the cathode material to store and release energy.

question: what is the main mineral in lithium batteries
gold_text: exchangers that are prone to corrosion. The reactors use lithium to counteract the corrosive effects of boric acid , which is added to the water to absorb excess neutrons. [139] Medicine [ edit ] Main article: Lithium (medication) Lithium is useful in the treatment of bipolar disorder . [140] Lithium salts may also be helpful for related diagnoses, such as schizoaffective disorder and cyclic major depression . The active part of these salts is the lithium ion Li + . [140] They may increase the risk of developing Ebstein's cardiac anomaly in infants born to women who take lithium during the first trimester of pregnancy. [141] Lithium has also been researched as a possible treatment for cluster headaches . [142] Biological role [ edit ] Primary food sources of lithium are grains and vegetables, and, in some areas, drinking water also contains significant amounts. [143] Human intake varies depending on location and diet. Lithium was first detected in human organs and fetal tissues in the late 19th century. In humans there are no defined lithium deficiency diseases, but low lithium intakes from water supplies were associated with increased rates of suicides, homicides and the arrest rates for drug use and other crimes. The biochemical mechanisms of action of lithium appear to be multifactorial and are intercorrelated with the functions of several enzymes, hormones and vitamins, as well as with growth and transforming factors. Evidence now appears to be sufficient to accept lithium as essential; a provisional RDA of 1,000 µg/day is suggested for a 70 kg adult. [143] [144] Precautions [ edit ] NFPA 704 fire diamond 3 2 2 W Fire diamond hazard sign for lithium metal [145] Lithium is corrosive and requires special handling to avoid skin contact. Breathing lithium dust or lithium compounds (which are often alkaline) initially irritate the nose and throat, while higher exposure can cause a buildup of fluid in the lungs , leading to pulmonary edema . The metal itself is a handling hazard because contact with moisture produces the caustic lithium hydroxide. Lithium is safely stored in non-reactive compounds such as naphtha . [146] Regulation [ edit ] Some jurisdictions limit the sale of lithium batteries , which are the most readily available source of lithium for ordinary consumers. Lithium
model_answer: The main mineral in lithium batteries is lithium itself, in the form of lithium ions (Li+). These ions are used in the cathode of the battery, where they are combined with other materials to form a compound that stores and releases energy.

question: what is the main mineral in lithium batteries
gold_text: exchangers that are prone to corrosion. The reactors use lithium to counteract the corrosive effects of boric acid , which is added to the water to absorb excess neutrons. [139] Medicine [ edit ] Main article: Lithium (medication) Lithium is useful in the treatment of bipolar disorder . [140] Lithium salts may also be helpful for related diagnoses, such as schizoaffective disorder and cyclic major depression . The active part of these salts is the lithium ion Li + . [140] They may increase the risk of developing Ebstein's cardiac anomaly in infants born to women who take lithium during the first trimester of pregnancy. [141] Lithium has also been researched as a possible treatment for cluster headaches . [142] Biological role [ edit ] Primary food sources of lithium are grains and vegetables, and, in some areas, drinking water also contains significant amounts. [143] Human intake varies depending on location and diet. Lithium was first detected in human organs and fetal tissues in the late 19th century. In humans there are no defined lithium deficiency diseases, but low lithium intakes from water supplies were associated with increased rates of suicides, homicides and the arrest rates for drug use and other crimes. The biochemical mechanisms of action of lithium appear to be multifactorial and are intercorrelated with the functions of several enzymes, hormones and vitamins, as well as with growth and transforming factors. Evidence now appears to be sufficient to accept lithium as essential; a provisional RDA of 1,000 µg/day is suggested for a 70 kg adult. [143] [144] Precautions [ edit ] NFPA 704 fire diamond 3 2 2 W Fire diamond hazard sign for lithium metal [145] Lithium is corrosive and requires special handling to avoid skin contact. Breathing lithium dust or lithium compounds (which are often alkaline) initially irritate the nose and throat, while higher exposure can cause a buildup of fluid in the lungs , leading to pulmonary edema . The metal itself is a handling hazard because contact with moisture produces the caustic lithium hydroxide. Lithium is safely stored in non-reactive compounds such as naphtha . [146] Regulation [ edit ] Some jurisdictions limit the sale of lithium batteries , which are the most readily available source of lithium for ordinary consumers. Lithium

gold_text: exchangers that are prone to corrosion. The reactors use lithium to counteract the corrosive effects of boric acid , which is added to the water to absorb excess neutrons. [139] Medicine [ edit ] Main article: Lithium (medication) Lithium is useful in the treatment of bipolar disorder . [140] Lithium salts may also be helpful for related diagnoses, such as schizoaffective disorder and cyclic major depression . The active part of these salts is the lithium ion Li + . [140] They may increase the risk of developing Ebstein's cardiac anomaly in infants born to women who take lithium during the first trimester of pregnancy. [141] Lithium has also been researched as a possible treatment for cluster headaches . [142] Biological role [ edit ] Primary food sources of lithium are grains and vegetables, and, in some areas, drinking water also contains significant amounts. [143] Human intake varies depending on location and diet. Lithium was first detected in human organs and fetal tissues in the late 19th century. In humans there are no defined lithium deficiency diseases, but low lithium intakes from water supplies were associated with increased rates of suicides, homicides and the arrest rates for drug use and other crimes. The biochemical mechanisms of action of lithium appear to be multifactorial and are intercorrelated with the functions of several enzymes, hormones and vitamins, as well as with growth and transforming factors. Evidence now appears to be sufficient to accept lithium as essential; a provisional RDA of 1,000 µg/day is suggested for a 70 kg adult. [143] [144] Precautions [ edit ] NFPA 704 fire diamond 3 2 2 W Fire diamond hazard sign for lithium metal [145] Lithium is corrosive and requires special handling to avoid skin contact. Breathing lithium dust or lithium compounds (which are often alkaline) initially irritate the nose and throat, while higher exposure can cause a buildup of fluid in the lungs , leading to pulmonary edema . The metal itself is a handling hazard because contact with moisture produces the caustic lithium hydroxide. Lithium is safely stored in non-reactive compounds such as naphtha . [146] Regulation [ edit ] Some jurisdictions limit the sale of lithium batteries , which are the most readily available source of lithium for ordinary consumers. Lithium
model_answer: The main mineral in lithium batteries is lithium itself, in the form of lithium ions (Li+). These ions are used in the cathode of lithium-ion batteries, where they react with the cathode material during charging and discharging. The anode in lithium-ion batteries is typically made of carbon, and the electrolyte is a lithium salt in a solvent.

gold_text: exchangers that are prone to corrosion. The reactors use lithium to counteract the corrosive effects of boric acid , which is added to the water to absorb excess neutrons. [139] Medicine [ edit ] Main article: Lithium (medication) Lithium is useful in the treatment of bipolar disorder . [140] Lithium salts may also be helpful for related diagnoses, such as schizoaffective disorder and cyclic major depression . The active part of these salts is the lithium ion Li + . [140] They may increase the risk of developing Ebstein's cardiac anomaly in infants born to women who take lithium during the first trimester of pregnancy. [141] Lithium has also been researched as a possible treatment for cluster headaches . [142] Biological role [ edit ] Primary food sources of lithium are grains and vegetables, and, in some areas, drinking water also contains significant amounts. [143] Human intake varies depending on location and diet. Lithium was first detected in human organs and fetal tissues in the late 19th century. In humans there are no defined lithium deficiency diseases, but low lithium intakes from water supplies were associated with increased rates of suicides, homicides and the arrest rates for drug use and other crimes. The biochemical mechanisms of action of lithium appear to be multifactorial and are intercorrelated with the functions of several enzymes, hormones and vitamins, as well as with growth and transforming factors. Evidence now appears to be sufficient to accept lithium as essential; a provisional RDA of 1,000 µg/day is suggested for a 70 kg adult. [143] [144] Precautions [ edit ] NFPA 704 fire diamond 3 2 2 W Fire diamond hazard sign for lithium metal [145] Lithium is corrosive and requires special handling to avoid skin contact. Breathing lithium dust or lithium compounds (which are often alkaline) initially irritate the nose and throat, while higher exposure can cause a buildup of fluid in the lungs , leading to pulmonary edema . The metal itself is a handling hazard because contact with moisture produces the caustic lithium hydroxide. Lithium is safely stored in non-reactive compounds such as naphtha . [146] Regulation [ edit ] Some jurisdictions limit the sale of lithium batteries , which are the most readily available source of lithium for ordinary consumers. Lithium
model_answer: The main mineral in lithium batteries is lithium itself, in the form of lithium ions (Li+). These ions are used in the cathode and anode of lithium-ion batteries, where they participate in the electrochemical reactions that store and release energy.

question: what is the main mineral in lithium batteries
gold_text: exchangers that are prone to corrosion. The reactors use lithium to counteract the corrosive effects of boric acid , which is added to the water to absorb excess neutrons. [139] Medicine [ edit ] Main article: Lithium (medication) Lithium is useful in the treatment of bipolar disorder . [140] Lithium salts may also be helpful for related diagnoses, such as schizoaffective disorder and cyclic major depression . The active part of these salts is the lithium ion Li + . [140] They may increase the risk of developing Ebstein's cardiac anomaly in infants born to women who take lithium during the first trimester of pregnancy. [141] Lithium has also been researched as a possible treatment for cluster headaches . [142] Biological role [ edit ] Primary food sources of lithium are grains and vegetables, and, in some areas, drinking water also contains significant amounts. [143] Human intake varies depending on location and diet. Lithium was first detected in human organs and fetal tissues in the late 19th century. In humans there are no defined lithium deficiency diseases, but low lithium intakes from water supplies were associated with increased rates of suicides, homicides and the arrest rates for drug use and other crimes. The biochemical mechanisms of action of lithium appear to be multifactorial and are intercorrelated with the functions of several enzymes, hormones and vitamins, as well as with growth and transforming factors. Evidence now appears to be sufficient to accept lithium as essential; a provisional RDA of 1,000 µg/day is suggested for a 70 kg adult. [143] [144] Precautions [ edit ] NFPA 704 fire diamond 3 2 2 W Fire diamond hazard sign for lithium metal [145] Lithium is corrosive and requires special handling to avoid skin contact. Breathing lithium dust or lithium compounds (which are often alkaline) initially irritate the nose and throat, while higher exposure can cause a buildup of fluid in the lungs , leading to pulmonary edema . The metal itself is a handling hazard because contact with moisture produces the caustic lithium hydroxide. Lithium is safely stored in non-reactive compounds such as naphtha . [146] Regulation [ edit ] Some jurisdictions limit the sale of lithium batteries , which are the most readily available source of lithium for ordinary consumers. Lithium

question: what is the main mineral in lithium batteries
gold_text: exchangers that are prone to corrosion. The reactors use lithium to counteract the corrosive effects of boric acid , which is added to the water to absorb excess neutrons. [139] Medicine [ edit ] Main article: Lithium (medication) Lithium is useful in the treatment of bipolar disorder . [140] Lithium salts may also be helpful for related diagnoses, such as schizoaffective disorder and cyclic major depression . The active part of these salts is the lithium ion Li + . [140] They may increase the risk of developing Ebstein's cardiac anomaly in infants born to women who take lithium during the first trimester of pregnancy. [141] Lithium has also been researched as a possible treatment for cluster headaches . [142] Biological role [ edit ] Primary food sources of lithium are grains and vegetables, and, in some areas, drinking water also contains significant amounts. [143] Human intake varies depending on location and diet. Lithium was first detected in human organs and fetal tissues in the late 19th century. In humans there are no defined lithium deficiency diseases, but low lithium intakes from water supplies were associated with increased rates of suicides, homicides and the arrest rates for drug use and other crimes. The biochemical mechanisms of action of lithium appear to be multifactorial and are intercorrelated with the functions of several enzymes, hormones and vitamins, as well as with growth and transforming factors. Evidence now appears to be sufficient to accept lithium as essential; a provisional RDA of 1,000 µg/day is suggested for a 70 kg adult. [143] [144] Precautions [ edit ] NFPA 704 fire diamond 3 2 2 W Fire diamond hazard sign for lithium metal [145] Lithium is corrosive and requires special handling to avoid skin contact. Breathing lithium dust or lithium compounds (which are often alkaline) initially irritate the nose and throat, while higher exposure can cause a buildup of fluid in the lungs , leading to pulmonary edema . The metal itself is a handling hazard because contact with moisture produces the caustic lithium hydroxide. Lithium is safely stored in non-reactive compounds such as naphtha . [146] Regulation [ edit ] Some jurisdictions limit the sale of lithium batteries , which are the most readily available source of lithium for ordinary consumers. Lithium

question: what was the name of the plant on little shop of horrors
gold_text: a little" by her sadistic , mean-spirited boyfriend Orin Scrivello ( Steve Martin ). The three girls suggest Audrey dump Orin and get another man to protect her, like Seymour, but Audrey states she doesn't deserve a nice guy. Despite this, Audrey has feelings for Seymour and secretly dreams of running off with him to the suburbs ("Somewhere That's Green"). Audrey II continues to grow rapidly and Seymour becomes a local celebrity ("Some Fun Now"). Seymour soon attempts to ask Audrey out, but she turns him down because she has a date with her boyfriend, revealed to be a dentist ("Dentist!"). After Seymour closes up shop, Audrey II begins to talk to Seymour, demanding more blood than Seymour can give. The plant proposes that Seymour murder someone in exchange for fame and fortune: Seymour initially refuses, but agrees after witnessing Orin beating Audrey ("Feed Me (Get It)"). After Orin finishes with his masochistic patient, Arthur Denton ( Bill Murray ), who requested "a long, slow, root canal", Seymour books an appointment with Orin and arms himself with a revolver; however, he cannot bring himself to use it. Orin, who abuses nitrous oxide, puts on a type of venturi mask to receive a constant flow of the gas. Accidentally breaking an intake valve and unable to remove the mask, Orin begs Seymour for help removing it, but Seymour does nothing. When Orin asks Seymour what he ever did to him, Seymour coldly replies, "Nothing, it's what you did to her." Orin dies from asphyxiation and Seymour drags his body back to Audrey II. While dismembering the body to feed to the plant, Seymour is unknowingly witnessed by Mushnik, who flees in fear. After feeding Orin's parts to Audrey II, which has grown to enormous size, Seymour discovers the police investigating Orin's disappearance. Arachidonic acid is a fatty acid found in cell membranes, particularly in the phospholipids of the plasma membrane. It is one of the polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) and is an essential fatty acid, meaning it cannot be synthesized by the human body and must be obtained through diet.

In the body, arachidonic acid is metabolized by various enzymes to produce a wide range of biologically active compounds known as eicosanoids. These eicosanoids play crucial roles in various physiological processes, including inflammation, blood clotting, and the regulation of blood pressure.

The metabolism of arachidonic acid can be initiated by the action of phospholipases, enzymes that break down phospholipids. Two types of phospholipases are particularly important in this context: cytosolic phospholipase A2 (cPLA2) and secretory phospholipase A2 (sPLA2). cPLA2 releases arachidonic acid from the membrane, while sPLA2 is involved in the release of arachidonic acid from extracellular membranes.

Once released, arachidonic acid can be metabolized by enzymes such as cyclooxygenase (COX), lipoxygenase (LOX), and cytochrome P450 enzymes. These enzymes convert arachidonic acid into various eicosanoids, including prostaglandins, leukotrienes, and thromboxanes. These eicosanoids, in turn, play important roles in inflammation, pain, fever, and blood clotting.

In summary, arachidonic acid is an essential fatty acid found in cell membranes. It is metabolized by various enzymes to produce eicosanoids, which are involved in a wide range of physiological processes. The metabolism of arachidonic acid is initiated by the action of phospholipases, with cPLA2 and sPLA2 being particularly important in this context.

model_answer: Arachidonic acid is a fatty acid that is found in cell membranes, particularly in the phospholipids of the membrane. It is released from the membrane by the action of certain enzymes, such as cytosolic phospholipase A2 (cPLA2) and secretory PLA2 (sPLA2), and then metabolized by various enzymes to produce a wide range of eicosanoids and metabolites. These eicosanoids include prostaglandins, prostacyclin, thromboxanes, leukotrienes, and others. The metabolism of arachidonic acid is a complex process that involves several enzymes, including cyclooxygenase (COX)-1 and COX-2, 5-lipoxygenase, and 15-lipoxygenase-1 and 15-lipoxygenase-2. These enzymes convert arachidonic acid into various bioactive compounds that play important roles in inflammation, pain, blood clotting, and other physiological processes.

model_answer: Arachidonic acid is a fatty acid that is found in the membrane of cellular phospholipids. It is released from these phospholipids by the action of enzymes such as cytosolic phospholipase A2 (cPLA2) and secretory PLA2 (sPLA2). Once released, arachidonic acid can be metabolized by various enzymes to produce a wide range of eicosanoids and metabolites, including prostaglandins, prostacyclin, thromboxanes, leukotrienes, and 12-Hydroxyheptadecatrienoic acid (12-HHT). These eicosanoids play important roles in various physiological processes, such as inflammation, pain, and blood clotting.

model_answer: Arachidonic acid is a fatty acid found in cell membranes, particularly in the phospholipids of the membrane. It is released from these phospholipids by the action of phospholipases, specifically cytosolic phospholipase A2 (cPLA2) and secretory PLA2 (sPLA2). Once released, arachidonic acid can be metabolized by various enzymes to produce a wide range of eicosanoids, including prostaglandins, prostacyclin, thromboxanes, leukotrienes, and others. These eicosanoids play important roles in various physiological processes, such as inflammation, pain, blood clotting, and immune response.

model_answer: Arachidonic acid is a fatty acid that is found in the membrane of cellular phospholipids, particularly in the phospholipid known as phosphatidylcholine. It is released from these phospholipids by the action of enzymes such as cytosolic phospholipase A2 (cPLA2) and secretory PLA2 (sPLA2). Once released, arachidonic acid can be metabolized by various enzymes to produce a wide range of eicosanoids, including prostaglandins, prostacyclin, thromboxanes, leukotrienes, and others. These eicosanoids play important roles in various physiological processes, such as inflammation, pain, blood clotting, and immune response.

Arachidonic acid is a fatty acid found in cell membranes, particularly in the phospholipids of the plasma membrane. It is a precursor to various eicosanoids, which are signaling molecules that play crucial roles in inflammation, blood clotting, and other physiological processes.

In the body, arachidonic acid is released from membrane phospholipids by the action of phospholipases, specifically cytosolic phospholipase A2 (cPLA2) and secretory phospholipase A2 (sPLA2). cPLA2 releases arachidonic acid from membranes within cells, while sPLA2 is secreted by cells and acts on extracellular membranes.

Once released, arachidonic acid is metabolized by various enzymes to produce a wide range of eicosanoids. The enzymes cyclooxygenase (COX) and lipoxygenase (LOX) are particularly important in this process. COX metabolizes arachidonic acid to prostaglandins, prostacyclin, and thromboxanes, while LOX produces leukotrienes and hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acids (HETEs).

Prostaglandins, prostacyclin, and thromboxanes are involved in regulating blood flow, platelet aggregation, and pain perception, among other functions. Leukotrienes and HETEs are involved in inflammation, allergic reactions, and other immune responses.

In summary, arachidonic acid is a fatty acid found in cell membranes that is released by phospholipases and metabolized by enzymes such as COX and LOX to produce a variety of eicosanoids, which are signaling molecules that play important roles in various physiological processes.

model_answer: Arachidonic acid is a fatty acid that is found in the membrane of cellular phospholipids. It is released from these phospholipids by the action of cytosolic phospholipase A2 (cPLA2) or secretory PLA2 (sPLA2). Once released, arachidonic acid is metabolized by various enzymes to produce a wide range of eicosanoids and metabolites, including prostaglandins, prostacyclin, thromboxanes, leukotrienes, and 12-Hydroxyheptadecatrienoic acid (12-HHT), among others. These eicosanoids play important roles in various physiological processes, such as inflammation, pain, blood clotting, and immune response.

model_answer: Arachidonic acid is a fatty acid that is found in cell membranes, particularly in the phospholipids of the membrane. It is released from these membranes by the action of enzymes such as cytosolic phospholipase A2 (cPLA2) and secretory PLA2 (sPLA2). Once released, arachidonic acid can be metabolized by various enzymes to produce a wide range of eicosanoids and metabolites, including prostaglandins, prostacyclin, thromboxanes, leukotrienes, and 12-Hydroxyheptadecatrienoic acid (12-HHT), among others. These eicosanoids play important roles in various physiological processes, such as inflammation, pain, and blood clotting.

model_answer: Arachidonic acid is a fatty acid that is found in the membrane of cellular phospholipids. It is released from these phospholipids by the action of cytosolic phospholipase A2 (cPLA2) or secretory PLA2 (sPLA2). Once released, arachidonic acid is metabolized by various enzymes to produce a wide range of eicosanoids and metabolites, including prostaglandins, prostacyclin, thromboxanes, leukotrienes, and 12-Hydroxyheptadecatrienoic acid (12-HHT), among others. These eicosanoids play crucial roles in various physiological processes, such as inflammation, pain, blood clotting, and immune response.

model_answer: Arachidonic acid is a fatty acid that is found in cell membranes, particularly in the phospholipids of the membrane. It is released from these membranes by the action of certain enzymes, such as cytosolic phospholipase A2 (cPLA2) and secretory PLA2 (sPLA2), and then metabolized by various enzymes to produce a wide range of biologically and clinically important eicosanoids and metabolites. These eicosanoids include prostaglandins, prostacyclin, thromboxanes, leukotrienes, and others. The metabolism of arachidonic acid is a complex process that involves several enzymes, including cyclooxygenase (COX)-1 and COX-2, 5-lipoxygenase, and 15-lipoxygenase-1 and 15-lipoxygenase-2.

model_answer: Arachidonic acid is found in the body as a component of phospholipids, particularly in cell membranes. It can be released from these membranes by the action of certain enzymes, such as cytosolic phospholipase A2 (cPLA2) and secretory PLA2 (sPLA2), and then metabolized into various eicosanoids, including prostaglandins, prostacyclin, thromboxanes, leukotrienes, and others. This metabolism is carried out by enzymes such as cyclooxygenase (COX)-1 and COX-2, 5-lipoxygenase, and 15-lipoxygenase-1 and -2.

model_answer: Arachidonic acid is a fatty acid found in cell membranes, particularly in the phospholipids of the membrane. It is released from these membranes by the action of certain enzymes, such as cytosolic phospholipase A2 (cPLA2) and secretory PLA2 (sPLA2), and then metabolized by enzymes like cyclooxygenase (COX), lipoxygenase, and others to produce various eicosanoids, including prostaglandins, leukotrienes, and hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acids (HETEs). These eicosanoids play important roles in various physiological processes, such as inflammation, pain, and blood clotting.

model_answer: Arachidonic acid is a fatty acid that is found in cell membranes, particularly in the phospholipids of the membrane. It is released from these membranes by the action of certain enzymes, such as cytosolic phospholipase A2 (cPLA2) and secretory PLA2 (sPLA2), and then metabolized by various enzymes to produce a wide range of biologically and clinically important eicosanoids and metabolites. These eicosanoids include prostaglandins, prostacyclin, thromboxanes, leukotrienes, and others. The metabolism of arachidonic acid is a key process in inflammation and other physiological responses.

model_answer: Arachidonic acid is a fatty acid that is found in cell membranes, particularly in the phospholipids of the membrane. It is released from these phospholipids by the action of phospholipases, specifically cytosolic phospholipase A2 (cPLA2) and secretory PLA2 (sPLA2). Once released, arachidonic acid can be metabolized by various enzymes to produce a wide range of eicosanoids, including prostaglandins, prostacyclin, thromboxanes, leukotrienes, and others. These eicosanoids play important roles in various physiological processes, such as inflammation, pain, blood clotting, and immune response.

model_answer: Arachidonic acid is a fatty acid that is found in cell membranes, particularly in the phospholipids of the membrane. It is released from these membranes by the action of certain enzymes, such as cytosolic phospholipase A2 (cPLA2) and secretory PLA2 (sPLA2), and then metabolized by various enzymes to produce a wide range of biologically and clinically important eicosanoids and metabolites. These eicosanoids include prostaglandins, prostacyclin, thromboxanes, leukotrienes, and others. The metabolism of arachidonic acid is a complex process that involves several enzymes, including cyclooxygenase (COX)-1 and COX-2, 5-lipoxygenase, and 15-lipoxygenase-1 and -2. These enzymes convert arachidonic acid into various intermediates and final products, which have diverse biological effects.

The metabolism of arachidonic acid is a complex process that involves several enzymes, including cyclooxygenase (COX)-1 and COX-2, 5-lipoxygenase, and 15-lipoxygenase-1 and 15-lipoxygenase-2.

gold_text: aorta branches, and these arteries branch in turn, they become successively smaller in diameter, down to the arterioles . The arterioles supply capillaries , which in turn empty into venules . The very first branches off of the aorta are the coronary arteries , which supply blood to the heart muscle itself. These are followed by the branches off the aortic arch, namely the brachiocephalic artery , the left common carotid , and the left subclavian arteries. Capillaries [ edit ] Main article: Capillaries The capillaries are the smallest of the blood vessels and are part of the microcirculation . The capillaries have a width of a single cell in diameter to aid in the fast and easy diffusion of gases, sugars and nutrients to surrounding tissues. Capillaries have no smooth muscle surrounding them and have a diameter less than that of red blood cells ; a red blood cell is typically 7 micrometers outside diameter, capillaries typically 5 micrometers inside diameter. The red blood cells must distort in order to pass through the capillaries. These small diameters of the capillaries provide a relatively large surface area for the exchange of gases and nutrients. Clinical significance [ edit ] Diagram showing the effects of atherosclerosis on an artery. Systemic arterial pressures, are generated by the forceful contractions of the heart's left ventricle . High blood pressure is a factor in causing arterial damage. Healthy resting arterial pressures, are relatively low, mean systemic pressures typically being under 100 mmHg, about 1.8 lbf/in², above surrounding atmospheric pressure (about 760 mmHg or 14.7 lbf/in² at sea level). To withstand and adapt to the pressures within, arteries are surrounded by varying thicknesses of smooth muscle which have extensive elastic and inelastic connective tissues . A blood squirt also known as an arterial gush is the effect when an artery is cut due to the higher arterial pressures.
